editorNote: The telephone line is becoming a software shelf: this week freely shared programs reach a mass audience while Atari changes hands and inventive games crowd the summer market.
morningLine: Public-domain programs dial into homes, Tramiel starts remaking Atari, and Shadowkeep crosses from disk to novel.

lead.headline: Free Software Travels the Phone Lines
lead.dek: Thousands of public-domain programs are moving through online services and local bulletin boards, challenging the idea that every useful disk must arrive in a shrink-wrapped box.
body: A Macintosh communications program has become the calling card for a much wider movement. MIT-trained consultant Dennis Brothers wrote MacTEP after probing the new machine closely enough to make it talk over telephone lines, then gave the program away. CompuServe placed it before a reported 135,000 subscribers, and calls soon reached Brothers from Britain and the Dominican Republic.

TIME counted roughly 35,000 public-domain programs in circulation. CompuServe, The Source, computer clubs, and hundreds of dial-up bulletin boards are turning modems into delivery trucks, carrying utilities and diversions without the $40-to-$500 price tags common on commercial shelves.

Finding the programs is becoming a business of its own. Mike Cane's $9.95 Computer Phone Book lists more than 400 boards and networks, while the $8.95 Free Software for the IBM PC describes more than 600 programs. The directories promise to make a scattered underground of disks and phone numbers legible to ordinary owners.

The economics remain experimental. Some authors ask only for a contribution from satisfied users: PC World editor Andrew Fluegelman reportedly earned more than $100,000 through that approach. Others, including early modem-program author Ward Christensen, decline unsolicited money. Either way, the phone line now looks like a genuine alternative software channel.

stories.headline: Tramiel Takes Atari and the Ax Falls
body: Jack Tramiel's acquisition of Atari's home-computer and videogame divisions is already reshaping Sunnyvale. Electronic Games Hotline put the sale at $240 million, with Warner retaining the coin-operated division and Ataritel.

Within the first week, the newsletter reported broad layoffs and immediate cost-cutting. Three Tramiel sons and several former Commodore executives were expected to help lead the company, while announced products were temporarily put on hold.

The industry's first reading is that computers will receive greater emphasis. What that means for Atari's game machines and software partners remains uncertain, but the old organization has ended with startling speed.

stories.headline: A Fantasy Computer Game Becomes a Novel
body: Spinnaker's Shadowkeep is reversing the usual adaptation route: instead of turning a book into a game, the Trillium adventure is inspiring a novel by science-fiction author Alan Dean Foster.

Created by Ultrasoft, the game supports parties of as many as nine characters, with five professions and four races. High-resolution graphics, animation, and full-sentence or abbreviated commands frame its fantasy expedition.

The tie-in suggests that a computer adventure can supply a world substantial enough to travel into print, an early sign that the young medium's characters and settings may outlive the disk that introduced them.

stories.headline: BYTE Surveys the Small-System Frontier
body: BYTE's August number finds personal computing splitting into many technical directions at once. Its feature list ranges from the 65816 processor and FORTH-83 to Modula-2, UNIX benchmarking, and an early look at Framework.

The review bench is just as broad: Macintosh, IBM PCjr, Sanyo MBC-550, a Juki printer, and four Logo implementations for the IBM PC all share the issue. At a $3.50 cover price, the magazine reads like a field guide to a market whose standards remain unsettled.

bbsNote.headline: The Modem Opens a New World of Computer
bbsNote.summary: COMPUTE!'s August modem primer described falling prices, the shift from acoustic couplers to direct-connect units, 300 versus 1200 bps economics, and BBS culture, while TIME showed CompuServe, The Source, and hundreds of boards distributing programs by telephone.

posts.text: Anchor Automation's Jerry Hussong argued that 300 baud remained the intelligent, economical choice for chatting with friends or reading local boards because so much material was available at that speed.
TIME reported both networks maintained large collections of downloadable public-domain software; CompuServe exposed MacTEP to 135,000 subscribers.
COMPUTE! put the modem range at about $49 to $1,000+, down from an $80 low a year earlier and roughly $200 several years before; it predicted $300-$500 1200-bps units by year's end.

curiosity.headline: Add Another Coin to Keep the Laser Movie Flying
curiosity.summary: Mylstar's Us vs. Them conversion kit turned a M.A.C.H. 3 laser-disc cabinet into a science-fiction flight film with live actors and overlaid computer graphics.
curiosity.detail: The attraction promised multiple camera angles, San Francisco, Chicago, Hollywood and wilderness backdrops, an orchestral score, a vibrating seat, and a special continue feature inviting extra coins during play.
